QUESTION:
Which other drugs interact with Prednisone?

RESPONSE:
Short answer: the label excerpt you've given me here doesn't include a Drug Interactions section — it only contains the INDICATIONS and DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION portions of the prednisone label. So I can't cite interaction information from this document.

For a complete list, you'd need the full prescribing information (the PRECAUTIONS/Drug Interactions section) or a pharmacist/drug-interaction database.

For general background only (not from this excerpt), prednisone labels and standard references commonly describe interactions with:

• Drugs that speed prednisone breakdown (may reduce its effect): rifampin, phenytoin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine, ephedrine.
• Drugs that slow its breakdown (may increase steroid effects/toxicity): ketoconazole, itraconazole, clarithromycin, ritonavir/cobicistat and other strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, estrogens/oral contraceptives, grapefruit juice.
• NSAIDs and aspirin: increased risk of GI ulceration/bleeding; corticosteroids can also lower salicylate levels.
• Anticoagulants (warfarin): unpredictable changes in INR — monitor closely.
• Potassium-depleting agents (loop/thiazide diuretics, amphotericin B): additive hypokalemia; caution with digoxin because low potassium raises the risk of arrhythmias.
• Antidiabetic drugs and insulin: corticosteroids raise blood glucose, so doses may need adjustment.
• Vaccines: reduced response to, and risk from, live vaccines with immunosuppressive doses; also blunted response to inactivated vaccines.
• Other immunosuppressants (e.g., cyclosporine, tacrolimus): increased infection risk and mutual level changes; convulsions have been reported with cyclosporine.
• Neuromuscular blockers and cholinesterase inhibitors (e.g., in myasthenia gravis): risk of myopathy or worsening weakness.
• Quinolone antibiotics: increased tendon rupture risk.
• Isoniazid: corticosteroids may lower isoniazid levels.

Please verify against the full FDA-approved label and check your specific medication list with a pharmacist or prescriber before making any changes.
